question: How do generics, variance, and `out`/`in` modifiers work in Kotlin?
answer:
Kotlin declares variance at the declaration site: `out` marks a type parameter the class only produces, `in` one it only consumes.

• Invariant (the default) — `Box<Dog>` is unrelated to `Box<Animal>` even though Dog is an Animal.
• `out T` — covariant. A `Producer<out T>` only returns T, so a `Producer<Dog>` is usable as a `Producer<Animal>`.
• `in T` — contravariant. A `Consumer<in T>` only accepts T, so a `Consumer<Animal>` is usable as a `Consumer<Dog>`.

Use-site variance exists too: `Box<out Any>` in a parameter position is the equivalent of Java's `? extends Any` wildcard, and `*` is the star projection for when the argument genuinely does not matter.

Generics are erased on the JVM, so `is T` is normally impossible inside a generic function. `inline fun <reified T>` is the escape hatch — the compiler substitutes the concrete type at every call site, which is how `filterIsInstance<T>()` and most Kotlin JSON APIs get their signatures. Bounds (`<T : Comparable<T>>`) constrain what the parameter accepts.

question: What are inline functions and reified type parameters in Kotlin?
answer:
An `inline fun` is replaced at compile time with the body of the function copied into the call site. The lambda parameters are inlined too — no Function<...> object allocation, no extra invocation.

Why:
• Performance — avoid lambda allocation in hot loops.
• Non-local return — `return` inside an inline lambda returns from the ENCLOSING function.
• Reified generics — when a type parameter is `reified`, the compiler knows T at the call site and you can write `T::class`, `is T`, `as T`.

Downsides:
• Code bloat if overused — every call site copies the body.
• `noinline` opts out of inlining for specific lambda parameters; `crossinline` forbids non-local returns from a specific lambda.

question: What are property delegates? Explain `by lazy`, `by Delegates.observable`, custom delegates.
answer:
Property delegation hands a property's get and set to another object: `by` forwards every read and write to that object's `getValue` / `setValue`.

Built-in delegates:
• `lazy { ... }` — computed on first read; thread-safe by default, and `LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE` drops the synchronization when you know the access is single-threaded.
• `Delegates.observable(initial) { prop, old, new -> ... }` — a callback after every set.
• `Delegates.vetoable(initial) { ... }` — the same, but the lambda can reject the change.
• `Delegates.notNull()` — the substitute for `lateinit` on primitive types, which `lateinit` does not support.
• `by map` — back a property with a Map, handy for dynamic schemas and deserialization.

Custom delegates are easy: implement the `getValue` / `setValue` operators, or the `ReadOnlyProperty` / `ReadWriteProperty` interfaces. Kotlin also supports `provideDelegate` if the delegate needs the property name at construction time.

Android is full of them — `by viewModels()`, `by activityViewModels()`, `by remember` in Compose. Note that the SharedPreferences-backed delegate below is the classic teaching example, but new Android code stores preferences in DataStore; the delegate shape is identical, only the suspending API differs.

question: How do you write a type-safe DSL in Kotlin?
answer:
A type-safe Kotlin DSL rests on three features: lambdas with receiver, extension functions and the `@DslMarker` annotation.

• Lambda with receiver — `block: A.() -> Unit` makes `this` an `A` inside the lambda, so A's members are in scope without a qualifier.
• Extension functions — add builder verbs to a type for the duration of the block without touching its source.
• `@DslMarker` — restricts which receivers are visible inside nested builders, so an inner block cannot accidentally call an outer scope's method.

The pattern is always the same: a top-level function takes a lambda with receiver, instantiates a builder, applies the lambda to it, and returns the built result. `apply` does the last two steps in one call.

Known DSLs to name: the Gradle Kotlin DSL, kotlinx.html, Compose itself (`Column { Text("...") }`), Ktor routing and the Exposed SQL DSL. Kotlin 2.2 added context parameters, replacing the experimental context receivers, as another way to make a scope available without threading a receiver through every signature.

question: What are typealiases and when should you use them?
answer:
`typealias` introduces a name for an existing type. It does NOT create a new type — it's purely a compile-time alias the compiler resolves to the underlying type.

Good uses:
• Shorten complex generic types: `typealias Cache = Map<String, ByteArray>`.
• Clarify intent: `typealias UserId = Long` reads better than passing raw Long around.
• Function-type aliases: `typealias Validator<T> = (T) -> Result<Unit>`.
• Deprecate old names while moving toward new ones.

Limitations:
• Not a wrapper — `UserId` and `Long` are the SAME type. The compiler does not enforce that you don't mix them.
• For real type-safety use a value class (inline class) or a wrapper data class.

question: What are value classes (inline classes) in Kotlin?
answer:
A value class wraps a single value that the compiler erases at runtime, replacing the wrapper with the underlying value wherever it can.

• Declared as `@JvmInline value class Email(val value: String)`; the `@JvmInline` annotation is required on the JVM target.
• Wraps exactly one property, and may carry an `init` block for validation plus its own functions and operators.
• You get language-level type safety with no allocation in most positions.
• The compiler still boxes when the wrapper appears as a generic argument, a nullable type or an interface implementation — `List<UserId>` really does hold boxed objects.

Idiomatic uses: domain primitives (UserId, Email, Money), units (Px, Dp, Hz), and any place a bare `Long` or `String` invites mixing two things up. Compare with `typealias`, which is only a name and gives no safety at all.

`@JvmInline value class` replaced the old `inline class` modifier, which was deprecated in Kotlin 1.5 and is no longer accepted by current compilers — you will only meet it in old code. Value classes with more than one property are still an experimental preview, not something to rely on.

question: Your Kotlin module is consumed from Java. Which declarations need a `@Jvm...` annotation to look right on the other side?
answer:
Companion objects, default arguments, top-level functions and property annotations all compile into shapes a Java caller finds awkward, and the `@Jvm` family exists to fix each one.

• `@JvmStatic` — a companion or `object` member becomes a real static method. Without it Java has to write `Config.Companion.load()`.
• `@JvmOverloads` — generates the telescoping overloads that default arguments imply. On a custom View's constructor this is what makes the framework's two- and three-argument inflation work.
• `@JvmField` — exposes a property as a plain public field with no getter or setter, which is what a Java caller and some serializers expect.
• `@JvmName` — renames a function, or renames the file facade class with `@file:JvmName("Strings")`. It also resolves a platform clash, where two Kotlin functions erase to the same JVM signature.
• `@Throws` — puts the checked exception back into the signature so Java can catch it.

The other half of the answer is annotation use-site targets. A Kotlin property can generate a field, a getter, a setter and a constructor parameter, and an annotation lands on only one of them, so a field-targeting annotation from a Java library needs `@field:SerializedName("user_id")` and a getter-targeting one needs `@get:JsonProperty`.

Finally, nullability is enforced at the boundary: public Kotlin functions start with an `Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter` call, so a Java caller passing null gets a NullPointerException pointing at your function rather than a confusing crash three frames deeper.

question: What are context parameters in Kotlin, and what problem do they solve that an extra function argument does not?
answer:
A context parameter is a dependency a function declares but nobody passes at the call site — the compiler supplies it from whatever context is in scope.

• Declared above the signature: `context(logger: Logger) fun sync() { logger.info("start") }`. Any caller that is itself inside a `Logger` context compiles; anyone else gets an error saying the context is missing.
• A caller opens a context with `with(logger) { sync() }`, or by declaring the same context parameter and letting it propagate.
• A declaration can take several context parameters, and unlike an extension receiver they do not occupy the `this` of the function, so an extension can have both: `context(db: Transaction) fun User.save()`.

What it buys you is ambient dependencies that would otherwise be threaded through ten layers of signatures — a logger, an analytics tracker, a clock, a coroutine-free transaction handle — and scoped capabilities, where a function is callable only inside the right scope. A DSL uses the same idea to make `+` or `unaryPlus` mean something only inside its builder block.

Two boundaries to state clearly. This is compile-time resolution, not runtime dependency injection: it replaces parameter threading, not Hilt or Koin, and nothing is looked up in a container. And it is the replacement for the older, never-stabilized context receivers, which is why any tutorial showing `context(Logger)` without a parameter name is out of date. Context parameters arrived in preview and may still need the `-Xcontext-parameters` compiler flag depending on your Kotlin version.

question: Why does a smart cast survive `if (!s.isNullOrEmpty())` but disappear through an identical helper you wrote yourself?
answer:
The standard library function declares a contract, a machine-readable promise that tells the compiler what its return value implies about its arguments.

Without a contract the compiler treats your helper as an opaque call: it cannot know that a `false` return means the receiver was not null, so the smart cast dies at the call. `kotlin.contracts` lets you say so:

• `returns(false) implies (this@isNullOrEmpty != null)` — the shape `isNullOrEmpty` uses. There are `returns()`, `returns(true)`, `returns(false)` and `returnsNotNull()`.
• `callsInPlace(block, InvocationKind.EXACTLY_ONCE)` — the other half of the API, and the reason you can assign a `val` inside a `run` or `let` block and still have the compiler consider it definitely initialized. It also enables smart casts made inside the lambda to survive after it.
• `require`, `check`, `requireNotNull` and `checkNotNull` are all built on contracts, which is why `require(x != null)` narrows `x` for the rest of the function.

The rules and the danger:
• A contract must be the very first statement in the function body, and the function must be a top-level or non-open member with a body.
• The API needs `@OptIn(ExperimentalContracts::class)`.
• The compiler TRUSTS the contract and never verifies it. Declare `returns(false) implies (x != null)` on a function that can return false with a null and you have handed the compiler a lie, and the resulting NullPointerException lands nowhere near the mistake.

So contracts are worth it for a widely used predicate or a scope-function-like helper, and not worth it for a one-off.

question: The compiler refuses to build until you add `@OptIn(...)`. What is that mechanism, and when would you define your own marker?
answer:
Opt-in is a library author's way of marking an API as unstable or dangerous so that callers have to acknowledge it in writing before using it.

How it works:
• The author declares a marker: an annotation class annotated `@RequiresOptIn(message = "...", level = ERROR)` — the level decides whether use produces a warning or a compile error.
• A caller has two choices. Accept locally with `@OptIn(ExperimentalMaterial3Api::class)` on the function, class or file, which stops the requirement there. Or propagate by annotating their own declaration with the marker itself, which pushes the same decision on to their callers.
• A whole module can accept a marker in the Gradle build with `compilerOptions.optIn.add("kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi")`, which is the sane choice for a marker you hit on every screen.

Markers you meet daily: `ExperimentalMaterial3Api` on half of Material 3, `ExperimentalCoroutinesApi` on things like `flatMapLatest`, and `DelicateCoroutinesApi` on `GlobalScope`, whose message says the API is stable but easy to misuse.

Opt-in is not deprecation. `@Deprecated` means this is going away; a requirement marker means this works today and its signature or behaviour may change without the usual compatibility promise.

Define your own when you publish a module and want a public-but-unstable surface, when a genuinely dangerous API needs a conscious decision at each call site, or when a shared library needs an internal escape hatch that is technically public because several modules use it.

question: A property typed `String` held null at runtime and crashed. How did a null get past the compiler?
answer:
Kotlin's non-null guarantee only covers code the Kotlin compiler checked, so nulls arrive from Java, from reflection and from assertions you wrote yourself.

The realistic sources, in the order they bite:
• Platform types. A value from unannotated Java arrives as `String!`, and the compiler lets you treat it as non-null with no check at all. Annotate the Java side, or convert at the boundary and keep the interior honest.
• Reflection-based JSON. Gson builds objects with Unsafe, skipping constructors entirely, so a missing field leaves `val name: String` null and default arguments are ignored. Moshi with codegen or kotlinx.serialization both generate real constructor calls and reject the missing field instead.
• `!!` and `lateinit`, which are assertions rather than proofs.
• An unbounded generic. In `fun <T> firstOrNull(): T` the parameter `T` can be inferred as a nullable type, so `T` is not automatically non-null — write `<T : Any>` when it must be.
• Java collections and arrays whose element type is a platform type, including `Map.get` on a Java map.

Kotlin does defend the boundary: every public function starts with `Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter`, so a null crossing from Java throws immediately with the parameter name, which is why such stack traces point at the first line of your function rather than somewhere deep inside it.

The engineering answer is to validate once, at the edge — parse network and database rows into your own types, decide there what a missing field means, and let the rest of the codebase trust its declarations.

question: In `sealed interface UiState<out T>`, why is `data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>` legal and useful?
answer:
`Nothing` has no instances at all and sits at the bottom of the type hierarchy, so with a covariant parameter `UiState<Nothing>` is a subtype of every `UiState<T>`.

That combination is why one shared `Loading` singleton fits a `UiState<User>`, a `UiState<List<Post>>` and everything else. Take the `out` away and it stops compiling, because an invariant `UiState<Nothing>` is unrelated to `UiState<User>`.

What `Nothing` is:
• The type with no values, and a subtype of every other type — the mirror image of `Any?` at the top.
• The type of `throw`, which is what lets `val x = value ?: throw IllegalStateException()` type-check, and the return type of `TODO()` and `error()`, which is why they compile in any position.
• A function declared to return `Nothing` never returns normally, so the compiler marks the code after a call to it unreachable and keeps smart casts alive in the surviving branch.
• `Nothing?` is the type of a bare `null`, and `emptyList()` is a `List<Nothing>` for the same subtyping reason.

Watch the variance rule when you extend this pattern: `out T` forbids `T` in an input position, so a `UiState<T>` may return a `T` but may not take one as a parameter. `data class Error(val cause: Throwable) : UiState<Nothing>` is fine because it does not mention `T` at all, and if you need a consumer instead, that is what `in` is for.
